subject: tech
title: Sending a Message
about: How a message gets from you to Grandma: the address says where it goes, the send button, the message travels in small pieces that are put back together before she sees it and a photo needs more pieces than words (K2-NI-01), it waits in the inbox to be read later while a video call is live, replies, read marks, emoji for feelings and voice messages. Only message people your family knows, a grown-up helps you send, read it again because you cannot take it back, wait kindly for a reply (K2-IC-03), and keep photos of yourself, your school and your address out of messages to people you have never met (K2-NI-03). Read it together, then send one real message to a family member.
tip: Help him send one real message to a grandparent: pick the address, type, read it again, send, then watch for the reply.

cards.q: You type Grandma's email address on a message. What does the address tell the tablet?
cards.note: An address says where the message goes, like the address on a letter. Each person has their own.

cards.q: You spell Grandma's address wrong. Does the message reach her?
cards.note: A wrong address sends it to the wrong place, or nowhere. A grown-up checks the address with you.

cards.q: Your message is all typed. Which button makes it go?
cards.note: Send is the button that lets the message go. Before send, you can still fix it.

cards.q: Why does a photo travel in many small pieces instead of one big piece?
cards.note: Small pieces slip through the wires and Wi-Fi more easily, and if one gets lost only that piece is sent again. Grandma's tablet puts them back together.

cards.q: You send a few words and a photo. Which one is cut into more pieces?
cards.note: A photo is much more data than a few words, so it needs many more pieces and takes a bit longer.

cards.q: Where does a new message wait until you open it?
cards.note: New messages wait in the inbox, like letters in a mailbox, until the person opens them.

cards.q: You send a message. Does Grandma have to read it right away?
cards.note: A message waits for her. She reads it when she has time and writes back later.

cards.q: In a video call, you talk and Grandma answers. When does she hear you?
cards.note: A video call is live. You see and hear each other at the same time, like being in the same room.

cards.q: Who is it okay to send messages to?
cards.note: Message only people your family knows: grandparents, cousins, friends your grown-ups know.

cards.q: You want to send a message. Who helps you?
cards.note: A grown-up helps you pick the address, type and send. Messaging is a together job.

cards.q: You tap send. Can you grab the message back?
cards.note: Once it is sent, the other person can see it right away. That is why you think before you send.

cards.q: Before you tap send, what is a smart thing to do?
cards.note: Read it again and ask: is it kind, is it right, is it going to the right person? Then send.

cards.q: You add a smiley face to your message. What does it show Grandma?
cards.note: An emoji shows a feeling that words alone might not. A smiley says I am happy.

cards.q: Grandma writes back to your message. What is her message called?
cards.note: When someone writes back, that is a reply. Replies go back and forth like a talk.

cards.q: A small word under your message says seen. What does that mean?
cards.note: Seen means the person opened your message. Seen or read marks can take a while to show.

cards.q: A game friend you have never met asks for a photo of you. What do you do?
cards.note: Photos of you are private, so never send one to someone you have not met. Stop and show a grown-up what they asked.

cards.q: You hold a button and talk, then let go. What did you send?
cards.note: A voice message records your voice and sends it. The other person taps play to hear you.

cards.q: Your cousin has not written back yet. What do you do?
cards.note: People are busy. Wait kindly, and do not send the same message again and again.
